FIG. S1. Non-Abelian quaternion charges and quasienergy bands in our 1D three-band Floquet models. (a) Schematic for calculating quaternion charges in the parameter space $(s_{12}, s_{13}, T, k_{x})$ . To avoid ambiguity in the quaternion charges induced by the sign of eigenstates, we start from a common basepoint $P_{0}$ and connect it to a target phase point $P_{1}$ as a reference path, along which all eigenstates are smoothly varied. We then connect the two equivalent points $P_{1}$ and $P_{2}$ to generate a $k_{x}$ Wilson loop. The quaternion charge is uniquely determined by the gauge choice that ensures a continuous evolution of the eigenstates along the $k_{x}$ loop. (b) Quasienergy band structures along the path A → G highlighted in Fig. 2(c), illustrating three successive transition points (TPs) from a trivial phase (point A) to an anomalous FNTI phase (point G). We also demonstrate eigenstate frame spheres for the four gapped phases (A, C, E, and G), where the Floquet eigenstates vary smoothly from $k_{x} = -\pi$ to $\pi$ . Red, green, and blue curves correspond to the eigenstates of the first, second, and third quasienergy bands, respectively. These results indicate that the four gapped phases carry quaternion charges $q = +1, +k, +j,$ and +1, respectively. For brevity, we do not distinguish the sign of quaternion charges $\pm i, \pm j,$ and $\pm k$ labeled in Fig. 2(d) (see main text).

FIG. S2. Phase diagram involved in Fig. 2(c), with the signs of the conjugacy classes $\{\pm i, \pm j, \pm k\}$ further specified. The red, green, and blue solid lines indicate the closures of the first, second, and third bandgaps, respectively.

Note: The quaternion charge can also be directly visualized from the eigenstate frame sphere of the $k_{x}$ -loop [1,2]. More concretely, for the trivial charge q = +1, the trajectories of the three eigenstates can be continuously contracted to three isolated points. In contrast, for the nontrivial charges $q = +i, +j$ and +k, the eigenstate frame rotates by $\pi$ around the red, green, and blue eigenstate trajectories, respectively, while their conjugate partners -i, -j and -k follow opposite rotations. Finally, for the nontrivial charge q = -1, the eigenstate trajectories rotate by an angle of $2\pi$ around the red, green, or blue eigenstate trajectories. The non-Abelian quaternion charge can also be theoretically calculated as follows. The charge for a Wilson loop is defined [1,2] as $Q = \exp[\oint \overline{A}(k) \cdot d\mathbf{k}]$ . Here, $\overline{A}(k) = \boldsymbol{\beta}(k) \cdot (-\frac{i}{2}\boldsymbol{\sigma})$ represents the spin Berry-Wilczek-Zee connection in the spin(3)-valued 1-form, with $\boldsymbol{\sigma} = (\sigma_x, \sigma_y, \sigma_z)$ being Pauli matrices, $\boldsymbol{\beta}(k) = -[A_{23}(k), A_{31}(k), A_{12}(k)]$ , and $A_{mn}(k) = \langle u_k^m | \nabla_k | u_k^n \rangle$ being Berry-Wilczek-Zee connection. The subscripts m and n (m, n = 1,2,3) label the energy bands from the lowest to the highest, and $u_k^n$ is the eigenstate of the nth band of the Floquet Hamiltonian [3]. The non-Abelian charges can be taken as $\pm\sigma_0$ , $\mp i\sigma_x$ , $\mp i\sigma_y$ , and $\mp i\sigma_z$ , which are represented by $\pm1$ , $\pm i$ , $\pm j$ , and $\pm k$ , respectively.

FIG. S3. Phase bands and the charges of their Dirac singularities $\overline{q}$ . (a) Phase bands plotted for phase E (with a topological charge $q = +j$ ). According to Jackiw-Rebbi's argument, the Dirac singularities in gaps 1 and 2 result in the emergence of TEMs in these gaps. (b) Enlarged views of the Dirac singularities. (c) Illustration of the method for calculating the quaternion charges of singularities. Starting from a common basepoint $P_{0}(k_{x}, t) = (-\pi, T)$ , we trace a reference path and construct

Wilson loops enclosing these singularities to obtain smoothed eigenstates of the phase bands. The ordered multiplication (indicated by the blue arrow) of these charges $\overline{q}_{m}$ equals the charge q of quasienergy bands (equivalent to the phase bands at t = T), i.e., $q = \prod_{m} \overline{q}_{m}$ . (d) Eigenstate frame spheres for these singularities. Their quaternion charges $\overline{q}_{2} = -\overline{i}$ and $\overline{q}_{1} = +\overline{k}$ satisfy the multiplication relation $\overline{q}_{2} \cdot \overline{q}_{1} = q = +j$ . (e)-(h) Similar to (a)-(d), but for phase G (anomalous FNTI) with a trivial charge $q = +1$ . The three Dirac singularities in the phase bands carry the charges $\overline{q}_{3} = -\overline{j}$ , $\overline{q}_{2} = -\overline{i}$ , and $\overline{q}_{1} = +\overline{k}$ , which satisfy the multiplication relation $\overline{q}_{3} \cdot \overline{q}_{2} \cdot \overline{q}_{1} = q = +1$ and suggest the emergence of three TEMs in the gaps.

Note: To introduce phase bands [3,4], we first review the full time-evolution operator $U(t) = \mathcal{T}e^{-i\int_0^t H(\tau)d\tau}$ . In our Floquet model, it can be expressed more explicitly as

$$
U (k _ {x}, t) = \left\{ \begin{array}{c} \mathrm{e} ^ {- \mathrm{i} H _ {1} t}, t \in \left[ 0, \frac {T}{4} \right], \\ \mathrm{e} ^ {- \mathrm{i} H _ {2} \left(t - \frac {T}{4}\right)} \mathrm{e} ^ {- \frac {\mathrm{i} H _ {1} T}{4}}, t \in \left[ \frac {T}{4}, \frac {3 T}{4} \right], \\ \mathrm{e} ^ {- \mathrm{i} H _ {1} \left(t - \frac {3 T}{4}\right)} \mathrm{e} ^ {- \frac {\mathrm{i} H _ {2} T}{2}} \mathrm{e} ^ {- \frac {\mathrm{i} H _ {1} T}{4}}, t \in \left[ \frac {3 T}{4}, T \right]. \end{array} \right.\tag{S1}
$$

To address the issue that $U(k_{x}, t)$ is not always PT-symmetric, we perform a smooth deformation to obtain a modified, PT-symmetric operator [3]

$$
\widetilde {U} (k _ {x}, t) = \left\{ \begin{array}{c c} \mathrm{e} ^ {- \mathrm{i} H _ {1} t}, & t \in \left[ 0, \frac {T}{4} \right], \\ \mathrm{e} ^ {- \frac {\mathrm{i} H _ {1} T}{8}} \mathrm{e} ^ {- \mathrm{i} H _ {2} \left(t - \frac {T}{4}\right)} \mathrm{e} ^ {- \frac {\mathrm{i} H _ {1} T}{8}}, & t \in \left[ \frac {T}{4}, \frac {3 T}{4} \right], \\ \mathrm{e} ^ {- \frac {\mathrm{i} H _ {1} \left(t - \frac {T}{2}\right)}{2}} \mathrm{e} ^ {- \frac {\mathrm{i} H _ {2} T}{2}} \mathrm{e} ^ {- \frac {\mathrm{i} H _ {1} \left(t - \frac {T}{2}\right)}{2}}, & t \in \left[ \frac {3 T}{4}, T \right]. \end{array} \right.\tag{S2}
$$

Formally, $\widetilde{U}(k_{x},t)$ can be expressed through spectral decomposition,

$$
\widetilde {U} (k _ {x}, t) = \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {3} \mathrm{e} ^ {- \mathrm{i} \phi_ {n} (k _ {x}, t)} | \psi_ {n} (k _ {x}, t) \rangle \langle \psi_ {n} (k _ {x}, t) |,\tag{S3}
$$

where $\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}\phi_{n}(k_{x},t)}$ is the eigenvalues of $\widetilde{U}(k_{x},t)$ and $\phi_{n}(k_{x},t)\in(-\pi,\pi]$ forms the phase bands. The $|\psi_{n}(k_{x},t)\rangle$ are real eigenstates that constitute the frame spheres. Obviously, $\widetilde{U}(k_{x},t)$ has the same phase band structures of $U(k_{x},t)$ because they are related by unitary transformations and satisfy $\widetilde{U}(k_{x},t=T)=U(k_{x},t=T)$ .

FIG. S6. Experimental measurement of quasienergy spectra (exemplified for phase G). (a)-(c) Fourier spectra performed for the data achieved by scanning cavity $i$ ( $i = 1 \sim 3$ ) of each unit cell, where the source is fixed at cavity $i$ of the middle unit cell of the sample. Only the 0-order sound signals are presented as an example, and high-order signals follow the same procedure. Note that we use (11), (22), and (33) to represent the excitation-detection at cavities 1, 2, and 3, respectively. (d) Complete quasienergy spectra (color scale) superposed from above three sets of data, which capture well the theoretically predicted quasienergy bands (white solid lines). (e)-(h) Similar to (a)-(d), but simulated from the coupled mode theory (CMT).

Note: Here we briefly introduce the calculations of temporal CMT [5]. The evolution of sound waves in a time-varying lattice can be described by a Schrödinger-type partial differential equation,

$$
- \mathrm{i} \frac {\partial}{\partial t} | \pmb {\Psi} (t) \rangle = H (t) | \pmb {\Psi} (t) \rangle + | \mathbf {s} (t) \rangle ,\tag{S4}
$$

where $H(t)$ is an $M \times M$ Hamiltonian matrix, with M being the total number of acoustic cavities. The vector $|\mathbf{s}(t)\rangle = [0, \ldots, \sqrt{2\gamma_j}e^{i\omega t}, 0, \ldots]$ represents the harmonic excitation at a frequency $\omega$ , where the non-zero term $\sqrt{2\gamma_j}e^{i\omega t}$ corresponds to the cavity containing the sound source. Applying the Floquet theorem [6,7], each term in the time-dependent wave function $|\Psi(t)\rangle = [a_1(t), a_2(t), \ldots, a_M(t)]$ can be expanded as a sum of $2N + 1$ Floquet harmonics,

$$
a _ {j} (t) = \sum_ {n = - N} ^ {N} A _ {j} ^ {n} \mathrm{e} ^ {\mathrm{i} (\omega + n \Omega) t}, \qquad j = 1 \sim M.\tag{S5}
$$

Finally, here $A_{j}^{n}$ represents the nth order Floquet harmonics, which can produce various of simulated results, such as transmission spectra in the binary cavity-tube structure, as well as quasienergy bands, topological edge mode (TEM), and topological interface mode (TIM) field distributions.

## Methods

Our static acoustic lattice was 3D-printed using photosensitive resin, which provides a rigid boundary condition due to its high impedance. To emulate three desired onsite energies, small square prisms were inserted into cavities 2 and 3 to fine-tune their resonant frequencies, while cavity 1 remained unchanged. Small holes were perforated in each cavity for inserting the sound source and probe, as well as for connecting circuit elements (cavities 1 and 3). To minimize sound leakage, unused holes were sealed with threaded stoppers during the measurements. Furthermore, to achieve time-periodic couplings $\mathrm{Im}(v_{13})$ and $\mathrm{Im}(v_{13}^{*})$ , 36 sets of carefully calibrated unidirectional coupling circuits are integrated into the static sample, based on the connections outlined in Fig. 3(d).

To demonstrate the implementation of dynamic couplings $[8-13]$ , we connect two sets of independent unidirectional coupling circuits to a simple binary cavity-tube structure, as illustrated by the color arrows in Fig. 3(e). Activating one set of circuits while deactivating the other, we measure the transmission response by exciting cavity 1 and detecting the pressure signal in the same cavity. Note that under the time-periodic modulation, each single-frequency excitation generates multiple harmonics spaced by 1/T (after performing a time-domain Fourier transform), as shown in Fig. S5. Experimentally, to prevent the mixing of different harmonics, we launched a series of quasi-monochromatic sound signals (spaced by 10 Hz) and measured their pressure responses individually. By extracting the amplitudes of different harmonic peaks, we obtain the transmission spectra responsible for the 0 and $\pm1$ orders [Fig. 3(f)], which are plotted against the excitation frequency $f_{in}$ . The emergence of high-order harmonic signals witnesses the implementation of dynamic couplings.

By carefully calibrating the phases and amplitudes of all circuit couplings, we generate accurate and spatiotemporally synchronized time-varying couplings across the acoustic lattice. To measure the bulk quasienergy spectra in Figs. 4(a) and 4(b), a sound source was fixed at the cavity $i$ ( $i = 1 \sim 3$ ) of the middle cell of the sample, along with a probe placed nearby for phase reference. Another probe was moved to scan the sound pressure in cavity $i$ across all unit cells [14-18]. (Again, we employ single-frequency excitation to distinguish different harmonics, and collect their weight information separately.) Performing a spatial Fourier transform for each harmonic, we obtain the $k$ -space sound energy distribution at given excitation frequency. Finally, sweeping the frequency gives the bulk spectra of different harmonics, each of which is plotted against the excitation frequency $f_{\mathrm{in}}$ . Finally, the quasienergy spectra were ultimately constructed by summing the three sets of data in energy [14-16]. (The reliability of these spectra was then assessed via a comparative study with the Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) approach [17,18], which yielded consistent results.) Similar procedures were applied to characterize TEMs [Figs. 4(c) and 4(d)] and TIMs [Figs. 5(d) and 5(e)], but with onsite excitation and detection across all cavities in the sample.
